name: Chipped, broken or knocked-out tooth
summary: A chipped, cracked or knocked-out tooth needs to be seen by a dentist. An adult tooth that has been knocked out has the best chance of being saved if it is put back or kept moist and seen within an hour.
redFlags: Head injury with the dental injury, such as being knocked out, vomiting or confusion
Bleeding from the mouth that will not stop after 15 minutes of pressure
Jaw that may be broken, or cannot close the mouth properly
Swelling making it difficult to breathe or swallow
urgentFlags: An adult tooth has been knocked out
A tooth is badly broken, loose or pushed out of place
Severe pain or a broken tooth with exposed pink or red inner part

commonCauses.title: Falls and sports injuries
commonCauses.detail: The most common cause of knocked-out or broken front teeth.

commonCauses.title: Biting hard objects
commonCauses.detail: Ice, hard sweets, bones or pen tops can crack teeth.

commonCauses.title: Tooth decay or large fillings
commonCauses.detail: Weakened teeth break more easily.

commonCauses.title: Teeth grinding
commonCauses.detail: Can crack teeth over time.

selfCare: Hold a knocked-out adult tooth by the crown (white part), not the root
If it is dirty, rinse it briefly in milk or saliva, then push it back into the socket and bite on a clean cloth
If you cannot put it back, keep it in milk or in your cheek and see a dentist straight away
For a chipped tooth, keep any pieces, rinse your mouth and see a dentist
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed, following the pack instructions
avoid: Putting a knocked-out baby tooth back in, as it can damage the adult tooth underneath
Scrubbing the tooth or storing it in water
Chewing on the broken tooth
seeDoctorIf: A tooth feels sensitive or has changed colour after an injury
A small chip has left a sharp edge
A filling or crown has come out

name: White patches in the mouth or oral thrush
summary: White patches in the mouth are often caused by oral thrush, a fungal infection that is easily treated. White patches that cannot be wiped off and do not go away should be checked by a dentist or doctor.
redFlags: Difficulty breathing or swallowing with mouth swelling
urgentFlags: Pain or difficulty when swallowing
A baby with thrush who is not feeding well
Thrush in someone with a weakened immune system

commonCauses.title: Oral thrush
commonCauses.detail: Creamy white patches that may wipe off, leaving red areas; more common with antibiotics, steroid inhalers, dentures or diabetes.

commonCauses.title: Coated tongue
commonCauses.detail: A harmless white coating from dead cells and bacteria, often with a dry mouth.

commonCauses.title: Lichen planus
commonCauses.detail: Lacy white patches on the inside of the cheeks or tongue.

commonCauses.title: Leukoplakia
commonCauses.detail: White patches that do not rub off; can occasionally become cancerous, so it needs checking.

selfCare: Ask a pharmacist about antifungal treatment for oral thrush
Rinse your mouth after using a steroid inhaler
Clean dentures every day and take them out at night
Brush your teeth and gently brush your tongue twice a day
avoid: Smoking
Sugary foods and mouthwashes containing alcohol while you have thrush
seeDoctorIf: Thrush has not improved after 1 week of treatment
White patches cannot be wiped off or keep coming back
A baby under 4 months has signs of thrush
White or red patches have lasted more than 3 weeks

name: Sore or burning tongue
summary: A sore tongue is often caused by biting or burning it, a mouth ulcer or irritation from food. It usually heals within a few days.
redFlags: Sudden swelling of the tongue, lips or throat, or difficulty breathing or swallowing
urgentFlags: Tongue pain with difficulty swallowing or speaking
A sore tongue with a high temperature and feeling very unwell

commonCauses.title: Injury or burns
commonCauses.detail: Biting the tongue or hot food and drink; should heal within a few days.

commonCauses.title: Mouth ulcers
commonCauses.detail: Painful sores can appear on the tongue.

commonCauses.title: Geographic tongue
commonCauses.detail: Harmless map-like smooth patches that can feel sore with some foods.

commonCauses.title: Low iron, vitamin B12 or folate
commonCauses.detail: Can make the tongue smooth, red and sore.

commonCauses.title: Burning mouth syndrome
commonCauses.detail: An ongoing burning feeling with no visible cause, more common after the menopause.

selfCare: Eat soft, cool foods and drink through a straw
Rinse with salt water (adults only) or ask a pharmacist about pain-relieving gels
Keep your mouth clean with gentle brushing
Sip cold water or suck ice chips
avoid: Spicy, acidic or very hot foods and drinks
Smoking and alcohol
seeDoctorIf: Tongue pain or itchiness does not go away or gets worse
You have white or red patches on your tongue
A sore or lump on the tongue lasts longer than 3 weeks

name: Loss of taste or changed taste
summary: Changes in taste are often linked to a cold, a problem with smell, a medicine or a mouth problem. Most of what we think of as flavour comes from smell, so the two often change together.
redFlags: Sudden change in taste with face drooping, weakness, numbness or slurred speech
urgentFlags: Taste change with facial weakness developing over a day or two
Unable to eat or drink enough because of taste changes

commonCauses.title: Colds, flu and COVID-19
commonCauses.detail: Usually linked to a loss of smell and recovers over weeks.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Many medicines, including some antibiotics and cancer treatments, can cause a metallic or bitter taste.

commonCauses.title: Mouth problems
commonCauses.detail: Gum disease, oral thrush, dry mouth and poor oral hygiene can affect taste.

commonCauses.title: Smoking and ageing
commonCauses.detail: Both can dull your sense of taste.

commonCauses.title: Nerve problems
commonCauses.detail: Bell's palsy or head injury can affect taste.

selfCare: Keep up good mouth hygiene, including brushing your tongue
Try foods with strong flavours, herbs and varied textures
Drink enough water to prevent a dry mouth
Stop smoking
avoid: Adding lots of extra salt or sugar to make food taste better
Stopping a prescribed medicine without talking to a doctor
seeDoctorIf: Your taste has not returned within 3 weeks
You think a medicine is causing taste changes
Taste changes are affecting your appetite or weight

sources.label: NHS – Lost or changed sense of smell

name: Cold sores
summary: Cold sores are small blisters on or around the lips caused by the herpes simplex virus. They are common and usually clear up on their own within 10 days.
redFlags: Cold sore near the eye with eye pain, redness or changes in vision
A newborn baby with blisters or who is unwell after contact with a cold sore
Widespread sores with high fever, confusion or drowsiness
urgentFlags: A cold sore near or in the eye
Swollen, painful gums and many sores inside the mouth, especially in a child
Cold sores with a weakened immune system or eczema around the sore

commonCauses.title: Herpes simplex virus
commonCauses.detail: Once you have the virus it stays in the body and can reactivate.

commonCauses.title: Triggers
commonCauses.detail: Colds and other illness, strong sunlight, tiredness, stress or periods can bring on a cold sore.

selfCare: Ask a pharmacist about antiviral cream, which works best when started at the first tingle
Use cold sore patches to protect the sore
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed, following the pack instructions
Wash your hands after touching the sore
Use lip balm with sun protection
avoid: Kissing, especially babies, while you have a cold sore
Oral sex while you have a cold sore
Sharing cups, cutlery, towels or lip balm
Touching the sore and then your eyes
seeDoctorIf: A cold sore has not started to heal within 10 days
The cold sore is very large or painful
You keep getting cold sores
You are pregnant and have a cold sore

name: Sore, dry or cracked lips
summary: Dry, sore or cracked lips are very common and are usually caused by cold weather, wind, sun or licking your lips. They usually get better with simple care.
redFlags: Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing
urgentFlags: Lips that are hot, painful and swollen, which could be an infection
Sore lips with mouth blisters, a rash and feeling unwell after a new medicine

commonCauses.title: Weather and dryness
commonCauses.detail: Cold, wind, dry air and sun dry out the lips.

commonCauses.title: Licking or biting the lips
commonCauses.detail: Saliva dries the lips further.

commonCauses.title: Angular cheilitis
commonCauses.detail: Sore, cracked corners of the mouth, sometimes from an infection or poorly fitting dentures.

commonCauses.title: Irritation or allergy
commonCauses.detail: Lipsticks, toothpaste or some foods can irritate the lips.

commonCauses.title: Dehydration and some medicines
commonCauses.detail: Not drinking enough, and acne or other medicines, can dry the lips.

selfCare: Use a lip balm, ideally with sun protection
Drink plenty of fluids
Ask a pharmacist about creams for sore corners of the mouth
Cover your lips with a scarf in cold, windy weather
avoid: Licking, biting or picking your lips
Lip products that sting or make things worse
Sharing lip balms or cups
seeDoctorIf: Your lips are not getting better after 2 weeks
Sore corners of the mouth keep coming back
A sore, lump or crust on the lip does not heal within 3 weeks

name: Wisdom tooth pain
aliases: swollen gum at back of mouth
summary: Wisdom teeth come through at the back of the mouth in late teens or adulthood. When there is not enough space, the gum over them can become sore, swollen or infected.
redFlags: Swelling in the mouth or neck making it difficult to breathe, swallow or speak
Swelling spreading towards the eye or down the neck
Unable to open the mouth with fever and feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: A swollen cheek or jaw
A high temperature with pain at the back of the mouth
Pus or a bad taste from the gum, with pain
Severe pain that painkillers do not control

commonCauses.title: Erupting wisdom tooth
commonCauses.detail: Pain and tenderness as the tooth breaks through.

commonCauses.title: Pericoronitis
commonCauses.detail: Infection of the gum flap over a partly erupted tooth, where food gets trapped.

commonCauses.title: Decay or gum disease
commonCauses.detail: Wisdom teeth are hard to clean, so they decay more easily.

selfCare: Rinse with warm salt water (adults only), especially after eating
Brush carefully around the area with a soft toothbrush
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Eat soft foods and chew on the other side
avoid: Leaving food trapped around the tooth
Smoking
Assuming the pain will settle if it keeps coming back
seeDoctorIf: Pain lasts more than 2 or 3 days
Pain keeps coming back
You find it hard to clean around the tooth

name: Teeth grinding or clenching
summary: Teeth grinding and jaw clenching often happen during sleep, and are linked to stress, anxiety, alcohol, caffeine and smoking. It can cause jaw pain, headaches and worn teeth.
redFlags: Jaw pain with chest pain, shortness of breath or sweating
urgentFlags: Jaw locking or being unable to open your mouth
A cracked or broken tooth with pain

commonCauses.title: Stress and anxiety
commonCauses.detail: The most common cause of grinding and clenching.

commonCauses.title: Sleep problems
commonCauses.detail: Grinding is linked to snoring and sleep apnoea.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol, caffeine, smoking and drugs
commonCauses.detail: These can make grinding worse.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some antidepressants can cause grinding.

selfCare: Try ways to relax, such as breathing exercises, exercise or a calming bedtime routine
Cut down on caffeine and alcohol, especially in the evening
Stop smoking
Practise keeping your lips together and teeth apart during the day
Apply a warm flannel to sore jaw muscles
avoid: Chewing gum or pens
Hard or chewy foods if your jaw is sore
seeDoctorIf: You grind your teeth and have tooth damage or sensitive teeth
You have pain in your jaw, face or ear
Your partner says you grind your teeth in your sleep
You are worried about your child grinding their teeth

name: Lump or red or white patch in the mouth
aliases: sore in mouth that won't heal
summary: Most lumps and patches in the mouth are harmless, such as a bitten cheek or a blocked saliva gland. Any lump, ulcer or red or white patch that does not heal within 3 weeks should be checked by a dentist or doctor.
redFlags: A swelling in the mouth or neck making it difficult to breathe or swallow
urgentFlags: A lump that is growing quickly
A lump with numbness of the lip or tongue
Bleeding from a lump or patch that does not stop easily

commonCauses.title: Minor injury
commonCauses.detail: Biting the cheek or lip can leave a lump that settles in a week or two.

commonCauses.title: Mucocele
commonCauses.detail: A harmless fluid-filled swelling, often on the lower lip, from a blocked saliva gland.

commonCauses.title: Gum boil from a tooth infection
commonCauses.detail: A small pus-filled lump on the gum near a painful tooth.

commonCauses.title: Leukoplakia or erythroplakia
commonCauses.detail: White or red patches that sometimes change into cancer.

commonCauses.title: Mouth cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common; risk is higher with smoking, chewing tobacco or betel, and heavy drinking.

selfCare: Keep your mouth clean and avoid irritating the area
Note when the lump or patch appeared and whether it changes
Stop smoking and cut down on alcohol
avoid: Picking at or trying to burst a lump
Waiting more than 3 weeks to get a non-healing lump or patch checked
seeDoctorIf: A lump, ulcer or patch has not healed within 3 weeks
A tooth has become loose for no clear reason
You have a lump in the neck as well
You have ongoing pain or difficulty swallowing

name: Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or face
summary: Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or face is often caused by an allergic reaction. If it affects breathing or swallowing it can be life-threatening (anaphylaxis) and needs emergency help.
redFlags: Lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swelling
Breathing very fast, struggling to breathe, wheezing, choking or gasping
Throat feels tight or struggling to swallow
Skin, tongue or lips turning blue, grey or pale
Suddenly very confused, drowsy or dizzy, or fainting
urgentFlags: Swelling of another part of the body, such as the hands or feet, that came on suddenly
Mild lip swelling that keeps coming back
Swelling that started after a new medicine

commonCauses.title: Allergic reaction
commonCauses.detail: To foods such as nuts or shellfish, insect stings, latex or medicines.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some blood pressure medicines (ACE inhibitors) can cause swelling, even after years of use.

commonCauses.title: Hereditary angioedema
commonCauses.detail: A rare inherited condition causing repeated swelling.

commonCauses.title: Local injury or infection
commonCauses.detail: A bite, burn or infection can cause swelling of one area.

selfCare: If you have a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector and signs of anaphylaxis, use it and call your local emergency number (such as 911, 999 or 112)
Lie down with legs raised, or sit up if breathing is difficult
For mild swelling without breathing problems, ask a pharmacist about antihistamines
Keep a note of anything you ate, touched or took before the swelling
avoid: Waiting to see if swelling of the tongue or throat gets better
Standing or walking about during a severe reaction
Taking the suspected trigger again
seeDoctorIf: You have had swelling and do not know the cause
Swelling keeps coming back
You think a regular medicine may be causing it

name: Cough
summary: A cough is usually caused by a virus such as a cold or flu and gets better on its own within 3 to 4 weeks. A cough lasting longer than 3 weeks should be checked.
redFlags: Severe difficulty breathing, gasping or unable to speak in full sentences
Lips or skin turning blue, grey or very pale
Coughing up more than a few streaks of blood
Cough with chest pain that spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back
Sudden confusion or very drowsy
urgentFlags: Cough is very bad or getting worse quickly
Feeling very unwell, or a high temperature that is not settling
Chest pain or finding it hard to breathe
Coughing up small streaks of blood
Swollen, painful glands in the side of the neck

commonCauses.title: Colds, flu and COVID-19
commonCauses.detail: The most common cause; the cough can last several weeks after other symptoms.

commonCauses.title: Chest infection
commonCauses.detail: Such as bronchitis, with a chesty cough and mucus.

commonCauses.title: Asthma and allergies
commonCauses.detail: Cough often worse at night or with exercise.

commonCauses.title: Acid reflux and postnasal drip
commonCauses.detail: Can cause a long-lasting cough.

commonCauses.title: Smoking and long-term lung conditions
commonCauses.detail: Such as COPD; a persistent cough needs checking.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Try hot lemon and honey (not for babies under 1)
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen for aches, following the pack instructions
Stay at home if you have a high temperature or feel unwell
Cover coughs and wash your hands often
avoid: Expecting antibiotics, which do not help viral coughs
Smoking
Giving cough medicines to young children unless advised by a pharmacist
seeDoctorIf: You have had a cough for more than 3 weeks
You are losing weight for no reason
You have a weakened immune system
Your cough keeps coming back

name: Coughing up phlegm or mucus
summary: Coughing up phlegm is common with colds and chest infections, and helps clear the airways. Yellow or green phlegm alone does not mean you need antibiotics.
redFlags: Severe difficulty breathing, or lips or skin turning blue or grey
Coughing up more than a few streaks of blood
Confusion, very fast breathing or feeling extremely unwell
urgentFlags: Feeling very unwell or symptoms getting worse
Blood-stained mucus
Fast breathing, chest pain or shortness of breath
Being over 65, pregnant, or having a long-term heart, lung or kidney condition with a chest infection

commonCauses.title: Chest infection (bronchitis)
commonCauses.detail: Usually viral and clears in 1 to 3 weeks.

commonCauses.title: Pneumonia
commonCauses.detail: Infection of the lungs with fever, breathlessness and feeling very unwell.

commonCauses.title: Postnasal drip
commonCauses.detail: Mucus from the nose running down the throat.

commonCauses.title: COPD, asthma or bronchiectasis
commonCauses.detail: Long-term lung conditions can cause daily phlegm.

commonCauses.title: Smoking
commonCauses.detail: Causes ongoing mucus production.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids to loosen the mucus
Breathe in steam from a warm shower
Raise your head with extra pillows at night
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever or aches, following the pack instructions
avoid: Smoking
Assuming coloured phlegm needs antibiotics
Cough suppressants for a chesty cough unless advised by a pharmacist
seeDoctorIf: Your cough has lasted more than 3 weeks
You keep getting chest infections
You cough up phlegm most days

name: Coughing up blood
summary: Coughing up blood can be caused by a chest infection or a nosebleed, but it can also be a sign of something serious. It should always be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Coughing up more than just a few spots or streaks of blood
Coughing up blood with difficulty breathing
Coughing up blood with a very fast heartbeat
Coughing up blood with pain in the chest or upper back
Coughing up blood with a painful, swollen leg
urgentFlags: A few small spots, flecks or streaks of blood in your phlegm
Blood in phlegm with a fever or feeling unwell

commonCauses.title: Chest infection
commonCauses.detail: A heavy cough can cause small streaks of blood.

commonCauses.title: Nosebleed or bleeding gums
commonCauses.detail: Blood from the nose or mouth can be mistaken for blood from the lungs.

commonCauses.title: Pulmonary embolism
commonCauses.detail: A blood clot in the lungs, often with breathlessness and chest pain.

commonCauses.title: Long-term lung conditions
commonCauses.detail: Bronchiectasis, tuberculosis or COPD.

commonCauses.title: Lung cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but more likely in smokers and older adults.

selfCare: Note how much blood there is and what it looks like
Arrange to be seen by a doctor even if it stops
avoid: Ignoring blood in your phlegm, even if it happens once
Smoking
seeDoctorIf: You have coughed up any blood that has not been checked
You also have a cough for more than 3 weeks or weight loss

name: Wheezing
summary: Wheezing is a whistling sound when you breathe, caused by narrowed airways. It is common with asthma and chest infections, and new or worsening wheezing should be checked.
redFlags: Severe breathlessness, unable to speak, eat or sleep
Lips or skin turning blue, grey or very pale
Reliever inhaler is not helping, or you need it more than every 4 hours
Wheezing with swelling of the lips, tongue or throat after eating, a sting or a medicine
Feeling drowsy, confused or exhausted from breathing
urgentFlags: Wheezing for the first time
Asthma symptoms getting worse, or needing your reliever more often than usual
Wheezing with a high temperature or chest pain

commonCauses.title: Asthma
commonCauses.detail: Airways become narrow and inflamed, often triggered by colds, allergens, exercise or cold air.

commonCauses.title: Chest infections
commonCauses.detail: Bronchitis and, in young children, bronchiolitis can cause wheezing.

commonCauses.title: COPD
commonCauses.detail: Long-term lung damage, usually from smoking.

commonCauses.title: Allergic reaction
commonCauses.detail: Sudden wheezing can be part of anaphylaxis.

commonCauses.title: Heart failure or acid reflux
commonCauses.detail: Less common causes of wheezing.

selfCare: If you have asthma, follow your personal asthma action plan and use your reliever inhaler as prescribed
Sit upright and try to breathe slowly
Avoid known triggers such as smoke, dust and pollen
Stop smoking
avoid: Smoking and second-hand smoke
Relying on your reliever inhaler without telling a doctor it is needed more often
Exercising hard while wheezy
seeDoctorIf: You have wheezing that has not been diagnosed
Your asthma is waking you at night or you use your reliever 3 or more times a week
Wheezing keeps coming back with colds

name: Shortness of breath
summary: Feeling short of breath is normal after exercise, but breathlessness that is new, sudden or getting worse needs medical advice. Sudden severe breathlessness is an emergency.
redFlags: Severe difficulty breathing: gasping, choking or unable to get words out
Chest feels tight or heavy
Pain that spreads to the arms, back, neck or jaw
Lips or skin turning very pale, blue or grey
Suddenly confused
Sudden breathlessness with swelling of the lips, tongue or throat
urgentFlags: More short of breath than usual
Breathlessness with feeling or being sick
Coughing up blood
Pain or swelling in one leg
A racing, fluttering or irregular heartbeat

commonCauses.title: Asthma or a chest infection
commonCauses.detail: Common causes of breathlessness with cough or wheeze.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety and panic
commonCauses.detail: Can cause fast breathing and a feeling of not getting enough air.

commonCauses.title: Being unfit or overweight
commonCauses.detail: Breathlessness on exertion that improves with activity over time.

commonCauses.title: COPD and other lung conditions
commonCauses.detail: Gradually worsening breathlessness, often in smokers.

commonCauses.title: Heart problems, anaemia or a blood clot
commonCauses.detail: Heart failure, anaemia and pulmonary embolism need prompt assessment.

selfCare: Sit upright, relax your shoulders and breathe slowly in through your nose and out through pursed lips
If you have asthma or COPD, follow your action plan
Stop smoking
Build up activity gradually if you are breathless because you are unfit
avoid: Trying to diagnose the cause yourself
Ignoring breathlessness that is getting worse
Smoking
seeDoctorIf: Breathlessness gets worse with normal activities or when you lie down
You are short of breath and have swollen ankles
You have been coughing for 3 weeks or more
You have been breathless for a while without a known cause

name: Chest pain or tightness
aliases: pain in left side of chest
summary: Chest pain has many causes and is often not caused by the heart, but it can be a sign of a heart attack. Sudden chest pain or pressure that does not go away needs emergency help.
redFlags: Sudden pain, pressure, squeezing or tightness in the chest that does not go away
Chest pain that spreads to the arms, neck, jaw, stomach or back
Chest pain with sweating, feeling sick, light-headed or short of breath
Sudden sharp chest pain with breathlessness or coughing up blood
Chest pain lasting 15 minutes or more
urgentFlags: Sharp chest pain that comes and goes, or only happens when breathing or coughing
Chest pain on exertion that eases with rest
Chest pain with a high temperature and cough

commonCauses.title: Muscle strain
commonCauses.detail: Pain after exercise, lifting or injury, worse when pressing the area or moving.

commonCauses.title: Heartburn or indigestion
commonCauses.detail: Burning pain after eating, often with a sour taste.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety or panic attack
commonCauses.detail: Sharp or tight pain with a racing heart, sweating and dizziness.

commonCauses.title: Chest infection or pleurisy
commonCauses.detail: Pain often worse on breathing in or coughing.

commonCauses.title: Heart problems
commonCauses.detail: Angina or a heart attack; pain often feels like pressure, heaviness or tightness.

selfCare: If you think it could be a heart attack, call your local emergency number (such as 911, 999 or 112), sit down and rest while waiting
If a pharmacist or doctor has said it is muscle pain, use heat and over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol, following the pack instructions
If heartburn is likely, ask a pharmacist about remedies and avoid large late meals
avoid: Driving yourself to hospital with chest pain
Assuming chest pain is indigestion without getting it checked
Exercising until chest pain has been assessed
seeDoctorIf: You have chest pain that comes and goes
You had chest pain that went away quickly but you are still worried
You get chest pain or tightness when walking or climbing stairs

name: Pain when breathing in
summary: Sharp chest pain that is worse when you breathe in or cough is often caused by a strained muscle or an infection, but it can also be a sign of pleurisy or a blood clot in the lungs.
redFlags: Sudden sharp chest pain with difficulty breathing
Coughing up more than a few streaks of blood
Very fast heartbeat with breathing pain
Chest pain spreading to the arms, back, neck or jaw
Breathing pain with a painful, swollen leg
urgentFlags: Sharp chest pain that comes and goes or only happens when breathing or coughing
Sharp chest pain that has not got better after a few days
Small streaks of blood in your phlegm
Feeling short of breath regularly

commonCauses.title: Muscle strain or rib injury
commonCauses.detail: Pain over a tender spot, worse with movement and deep breaths.

commonCauses.title: Costochondritis
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed cartilage where the ribs join the breastbone.

commonCauses.title: Pleurisy
commonCauses.detail: Inflammation of the lining of the lungs, usually from a viral infection.

commonCauses.title: Pneumonia
commonCauses.detail: Lung infection with fever, cough and breathlessness.

commonCauses.title: Pulmonary embolism or collapsed lung
commonCauses.detail: Serious causes that come on suddenly with breathlessness.

selfCare: Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Rest, and lie on the painful side if it helps
Hold a pillow against your chest when coughing
Take some slow, deep breaths each hour to keep the lungs clear
avoid: Ignoring sudden breathing pain with breathlessness
Heavy lifting or strenuous exercise until the pain settles
seeDoctorIf: Pain has not improved after a few days
Pain keeps coming back
You have had a recent injury and pain is getting worse

name: Heart palpitations
summary: Palpitations are when your heartbeat suddenly becomes noticeable, racing, pounding, fluttering or skipping. They are usually harmless and often linked to stress, caffeine or alcohol.
redFlags: Palpitations with chest pain
Palpitations with shortness of breath
Feeling faint or fainting with palpitations
Palpitations that do not go away
urgentFlags: You had palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness or faintness that have now stopped
A very fast heartbeat lasting more than a few minutes, even if you feel well

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety and panic
commonCauses.detail: Very common causes of a racing or pounding heart.

commonCauses.title: Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine and drugs
commonCauses.detail: Coffee, energy drinks, alcohol, smoking and recreational drugs can trigger palpitations.

commonCauses.title: Exercise, lack of sleep or hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Including pregnancy and the menopause.

commonCauses.title: Extra (ectopic) beats
commonCauses.detail: A harmless skipped or extra beat that most people have sometimes.

commonCauses.title: Heart rhythm problems and other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Atrial fibrillation, an overactive thyroid or anaemia can cause palpitations.

selfCare: Sit down and breathe slowly until they pass
Cut down on caffeine, alcohol and energy drinks
Stop smoking
Try relaxation such as breathing exercises, yoga or regular exercise
Note when they happen, how long they last and what you were doing
avoid: Recreational drugs and energy drinks
Driving while you feel faint or unwell
seeDoctorIf: Palpitations keep coming back or are happening more often
They last longer than a few minutes
You have a heart condition
There is a history of heart problems or sudden death in your family

name: Hiccups
summary: Hiccups are very common and usually stop on their own within a few minutes or hours. Hiccups lasting more than 48 hours should be checked.
redFlags: Hiccups with chest pain, shortness of breath or sweating
Hiccups with sudden weakness, numbness or slurred speech
urgentFlags: Hiccups with vomiting so you cannot keep fluids down
Hiccups stopping you eating, drinking or sleeping

commonCauses.title: Eating or drinking
commonCauses.detail: Large meals, fizzy drinks, alcohol and eating quickly.

commonCauses.title: Stress or excitement
commonCauses.detail: Strong emotions can trigger hiccups.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines, such as steroids, can cause hiccups.

commonCauses.title: Medical conditions
commonCauses.detail: Rarely, long-lasting hiccups are caused by reflux, nerve irritation or other conditions.

selfCare: Breathe into a paper (not plastic) bag
Hold your breath for a short time
Sip ice-cold water or bite on a lemon
Pull your knees up to your chest and lean forward
avoid: Fizzy drinks and alcohol
Eating very quickly or very large meals
Very hot then very cold food or drink
seeDoctorIf: Hiccups last longer than 48 hours
Hiccups keep coming back and are affecting your life

name: Blue or grey lips or skin
summary: Lips, tongue or skin that turn blue, grey or very pale can mean the body is not getting enough oxygen. When it comes on suddenly it is an emergency.
redFlags: Lips, tongue or skin suddenly turning blue, grey or very pale (on brown or black skin, check the palms, gums or around the eyes)
Blue lips with difficulty breathing or choking
Blue lips with confusion, drowsiness or collapse
A child who is blue, limp or not responding normally
urgentFlags: Fingers or toes that stay blue or white after warming up
Bluish lips that come and go with exercise

commonCauses.title: Cold
commonCauses.detail: Fingers, toes and lips can look blue in the cold and improve with warming.

commonCauses.title: Breathing problems
commonCauses.detail: Severe asthma, pneumonia, COPD or choking reduce oxygen levels.

commonCauses.title: Heart problems
commonCauses.detail: Heart failure or heart conditions present from birth.

commonCauses.title: Raynaud's phenomenon
commonCauses.detail: Fingers and toes turn white then blue in the cold or with stress.

selfCare: If someone suddenly turns blue or grey and is struggling to breathe, call your local emergency number (such as 911, 999 or 112)
If only fingers and toes are blue from cold, warm up gradually
avoid: Waiting to see if blue lips improve when someone is breathless or unwell
Smoking
seeDoctorIf: Your fingers or toes often change colour in the cold
Lips or nails look bluish with exercise or breathlessness

sources.label: MedlinePlus – Blue discoloration of the skin

name: Noisy or high-pitched breathing (stridor)
summary: Stridor is a high-pitched, harsh sound when breathing in, caused by a narrowed upper airway. It is most common in children with croup and should always be assessed, urgently if the person is struggling to breathe.
redFlags: High-pitched breathing with struggling to breathe or the skin sucking in between the ribs
Noisy breathing with drooling or unable to swallow
Lips or skin turning blue or grey
Noisy breathing after choking on food or an object
Sudden noisy breathing with swelling of the lips, tongue or throat
A child who is very drowsy, agitated or floppy
urgentFlags: Stridor in a child with croup, even if mild
A barking cough with a high temperature

commonCauses.title: Croup
commonCauses.detail: A viral infection in young children causing a barking cough and stridor, often worse at night.

commonCauses.title: Inhaled object
commonCauses.detail: Something stuck in the airway, especially in toddlers.

commonCauses.title: Allergic reaction
commonCauses.detail: Swelling of the throat in anaphylaxis.

commonCauses.title: Throat infections
commonCauses.detail: Rare but serious infections such as epiglottitis.

selfCare: Keep the person, especially a child, calm and sitting upright
Give fluids only if they can swallow easily
Get medical help straight away
avoid: Looking down a child's throat or putting fingers in the mouth if they are struggling to breathe
Making the person lie down
Steam treatments, which do not help croup and risk scalds
seeDoctorIf: Noisy breathing keeps coming back
A baby has noisy breathing that has not been checked
